title: July 2026 personal income and consumption rise while saving and spending composition remain separate household surfaces
source_unit: BEA National Income and Product Accounts monthly Personal Income and Outlays estimates

denominator.unit: aggregate US personal-income account; values are flows or rates, not household respondents

personal_income_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June; 0.4 percent monthly rate

disposable_personal_income_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June; 0.5 percent monthly rate

personal_consumption_expenditures_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June; 0.2 percent monthly rate

personal_outlays_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June

observations.method: BEA monthly National Income and Product Accounts estimate from the July 2026 Personal Income and Outlays release; personal outlays include PCE, personal interest payments, and personal current transfer payments.
observations.uncertainty: These are aggregate current-dollar national accounts, subject to revisions and the September 30 annual update; they do not identify households, real purchasing power, distribution, or causal sources of change.
observations.subgroup: Aggregate US personal sector; no household, income, age, race, place, or consumer subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: Aggregate income growth can be concentrated, offset by prices or taxes, or coexist with financial stress for particular households; current-dollar PCE is not a welfare measure.

denominator.unit: aggregate US personal consumption expenditures account

services_spending_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June

goods_spending_change.unit: billions of current US dollars from June

services_minus_goods_change.unit: billions of current US dollars; arithmetic contrast of reported changes

observations.method: BEA release decomposition of the $36.3 billion current-dollar PCE increase into services and goods components; the contrast is calculated from the reported component changes.
observations.uncertainty: The composition change is aggregate and current-dollar; it does not distinguish quantities from prices, essential from discretionary purchases, or substitution by household resources.
observations.subgroup: Aggregate US PCE by goods and services; no household or product-income subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: A rise in services spending and fall in goods spending can reflect prices, timing, seasonal patterns, supply, or reclassification rather than a cultural shift or household preference change.

denominator.unit: aggregate US disposable personal income account

observations.method: BEA personal saving and saving-rate estimates from the July 2026 Personal Income and Outlays release.
observations.uncertainty: The saving rate is an aggregate national-accounts ratio and is revised; it does not reveal liquid balances, debt service, precautionary motives, or the distribution of saving across households.
observations.subgroup: Aggregate US personal sector; no household or income subgroup.
observations.counterinterpretation: A change in aggregate saving can reflect income composition, transfers, tax timing, valuation or measurement revisions, and spending timing; it is not a direct measure of household financial resilience.

related_sources.claim: Federal Reserve SHED supplies household-level liquidity and saving-response context that aggregate BEA accounts cannot provide.
New York Fed supplies aggregate debt and delinquency context for household financial exposure.
BEA schedules the next Personal Income and Outlays release for September 30, 2026, when August data and annual updates are expected.

boundary: This record adds a current aggregate national-accounts surface for income, disposable income, consumption composition, personal outlays, and saving. It does not measure household-level purchasing power, financial buffers, debt stress, cultural meaning, firm pricing, political response, or causal effects. Current-dollar flows, aggregate ratios, survey respondents, and credit-record balances must remain separate.
